opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different structural advantages, and they compound in ways that matter a lot for research speed.

The most obvious one is just raw serial speed. If you have AI systems that are roughly as capable as a good human researcher but they think, say, five or ten times faster, then you get more serial work done per unit of wall-clock time. And a lot of research is bottlenecked on serial steps: you have an idea, you try it, you look at the results, you update, you try the next thing. Speeding up that loop matters a lot.

The second is parallelism and copying. Once you've trained a model, you can run a huge number of copies. You're not limited by how many people you can hire and onboard. Parallel labor has diminishing returns, since you can't just throw a million people at a problem and get a million times the progress, but it still helps a lot. You can explore many more directions, run many more careful ablations, and have copies doing the tedious stuff humans tend to skip.

Third, and I think people underrate this one, is the coordination and knowledge-transfer advantage. Human research orgs lose a huge amount of efficiency to communication overhead: meetings, getting someone up to speed, people leaving and taking context with them. AIs can potentially share context much more directly, and you can fork a copy that has all the relevant context instead of re-explaining it. You also don't have the same issues with motivation, fatigue, or people not wanting to do boring but important work.

Fourth, there's specialization. You can take one model and fine-tune or prompt it to be extremely good at a particular narrow sub-task, like writing kernels, debugging training runs, or analyzing experiment results, in a way that would take a human years to develop.

So how does that translate into actual speedup? My view is you can't just multiply these together, because you hit other bottlenecks, most notably compute for experiments. If you need to run training runs to learn things, faster thinking doesn't help much while you're waiting on the GPUs. But I think AIs can substantially mitigate that too: they can be much more careful about which experiments to run, run smaller-scale proxies more cleverly, and squeeze more out of each experiment, for instance by writing better, more efficient code.

Putting that together, my rough guess is that once you have AIs that can fully automate the work of top AI researchers, the speedup to algorithmic progress could plausibly be large, something like a 5x to 20x-ish acceleration in the overall rate of progress, maybe more, though with a lot of uncertainty. Even the conservative end of that is a pretty wild world, because it compresses what would have been years of progress into months. That's a big part of why I think the period right around full automation of AI R&D is so important to prepare for, both in terms of safety and in terms of how much time humans actually have to react.

r001.rationale: The response says faster AI thinking speeds the serial research loop, but it does not say AI researchers work around the clock or compare sequential experiments per year with humans.

r002.rationale: It describes sharing context and forking copies, but does not connect that advantage to handing subtasks to faster, weaker AIs.

r003.rationale: The response mentions faster execution and many parallel copies, but does not state that increasing execution speed reduces how many instances can run in parallel.

r004.rationale: It says a copy can be forked with all relevant context instead of re-explaining it, reducing human-style communication overhead.

r005.rationale: It explicitly identifies compute for experiments, especially waiting on GPUs, as a bottleneck that can limit the research speedup from faster thinking.

r006.rationale: It says parallel labor has diminishing returns and that a million people cannot produce a million times the progress, conveying that research cannot be perfectly parallelized.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on here, and it's worth separating them out, because they compound in a way that I think people often underrate.

The first one is just speed. Once you have an AI system that's roughly as capable as a good human AI researcher, it's probably running something like 10 to 50 times faster than a human in serial terms. That's not a crazy estimate given current inference speeds — we already have models that can produce tokens much faster than a human can type or think through a problem. So you've got this thing that can do a week of human cognitive work in a few hours.

The second one is the number of copies. And this is the thing I think is the biggest deal. If you look at the compute that frontier labs have, and you ask how much of it you'd need to run one of these systems at human-equivalent speed, you end up with numbers like — plausibly millions of parallel instances. The exact number depends a lot on the details, but even if you're off by a factor of 10 in either direction, it's a huge number relative to the current size of the AI research workforce, which is maybe on the order of thousands of people at the leading labs, if that.

So you're taking a field that currently has, say, a few thousand serious researchers, and you're saying: what if you had a million of them, each running 10 or 30 times faster? That's a massive increase in effective labour. And a lot of AI research is actually pretty labour-constrained right now. There are tonnes of experiments people would like to run, ideas people would like to try, engineering that would be nice to have done, and the bottleneck is often just that there aren't enough people with the relevant skills and context to do it.

Then there are some more qualitative things on top of that. The AI systems don't need to sleep. They can share knowledge much more directly — you can have one instance learn something and then that gets propagated to all the others, either through fine-tuning or just through much more efficient communication than humans manage. You don't have the coordination overhead of a large human organisation in the same way. You can run many instances on the same problem and have them explore different approaches in parallel without the social friction.

And they can be much better at some narrow things that matter a lot — like, they'll have read all of the ML literature, they'll have perfect recall of every experiment that's been run at the lab, they'll be able to write code very quickly and reliably. So even if the general reasoning ability is "just" human-level, the package is quite different from a human researcher.

Now, the obvious objection is: isn't this bottlenecked on compute for experiments? And I think that's partly right — you can't just scale up the number of researchers and get proportional speedups, because at some point they're all waiting on the same GPUs to run their experiments. But I think people overstate this. A lot of what makes research slow isn't the experiment itself, it's figuring out what experiment to run, debugging the implementation, analysing the results, deciding what to do next. If you compress all of that, you get a lot faster even at fixed compute. And you can also get much smarter about experiment design — running smaller-scale experiments that are more informative, extrapolating better, and so on. So I'd guess you still get something like a 10x speedup in overall AI progress, maybe more, even accounting for compute bottlenecks. And then that speedup itself feeds back into making the next generation of systems better, which is where things start to get really fast.

r001.rationale: It says AI systems do not need sleep, but does not connect this to completing more sequential experiments per year.

r002.rationale: It describes sharing knowledge among instances, but not transferable computational context when handing subtasks to faster, weaker AIs.

r003.rationale: It discusses faster execution and many parallel instances separately, without stating that faster execution reduces how many instances can run in parallel.

r004.rationale: It says parallel instances can avoid some coordination overhead, but does not describe forking them from a shared context as the means.

r005.rationale: It explicitly says compute constraints, such as researchers waiting for the same GPUs, prevent added research labour from producing proportional speedups.

r006.rationale: It attributes subproportional speedups to compute bottlenecks, but does not explain that research tasks themselves cannot be perfectly parallelised.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different advantages, and it’s useful to separate them. One is just that you could have a lot of AI researchers. Another is that each of them could operate much faster than a human. And then there are advantages in how they share information and coordinate.

So, suppose you have an AI that’s roughly as good as a strong human researcher, but it can do in an hour what would take that human a week. That lets you run through a sequence of ideas much faster: notice a problem, propose a fix, implement it, look at the results, and then decide what to try next. That’s particularly valuable because research isn’t just a bunch of independent tasks you can distribute to more people. Often you need the result of one thing before you know what to do next.

But there’s an important limitation, which is that the experiments don’t necessarily get faster. If you need to train a model for a month to test your idea, having the researcher think a hundred times faster doesn’t make that training run take a few hours. So the speedup depends on how much of the bottleneck is researcher time versus compute or waiting for experimental results.

Having lots of copies helps with the parallel parts. You can explore more approaches, inspect more failures, and do more careful implementation work. And potentially those copies can share what they’ve learned much more efficiently than humans can, though I wouldn’t assume that coordination is therefore free.

So I’d expect a substantial acceleration, but not one where you can just multiply the number of researchers by their thinking speed and get the speedup in AI progress. The key question is which parts of the research process remain bottlenecks once intellectual labour becomes much cheaper and faster.

r001.rationale: The response says faster researchers can move through a sequence of ideas more quickly, but does not attribute this to working around the clock or say they complete more sequential experiments per year.

r002.rationale: It mentions copies sharing what they learn, but does not identify transferable computational context for handing subtasks to faster, weaker AIs.

r003.rationale: It discusses faster operation and having many copies, but does not state that increasing execution speed limits how many instances can run in parallel.

r004.rationale: It says copies might share what they learn efficiently, but does not explain that forking instances from shared context could reduce coordination overhead.

r005.rationale: The response says researcher speed does not shorten a month-long training run and that acceleration depends on compute and experimental waiting bottlenecks.

r006.rationale: It explains that research is not a set of wholly independent tasks and often requires one result before deciding what to do next, limiting parallelisation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different advantages, and it’s useful to separate them. One is just speed: if you have an AI researcher that’s doing roughly the same cognitive work as a human researcher, but thinking ten times faster, then a project that would have taken a month might take a few days. That won’t apply to everything, because you still have to run experiments, but it can substantially shorten the parts where you’re deciding what to try or interpreting results.

Another advantage is parallelism. You can have a lot of copies working on different ideas, or have them independently check a proposed result. And those copies can potentially share information much more efficiently than humans. If one discovers a useful technique, you might be able to propagate that across the whole workforce without everyone having to learn it separately.

But I think you have to be careful about translating those advantages directly into a rate of progress. A thousand researchers don’t necessarily make progress a thousand times faster. They might all pursue correlated ideas, and some experiments require a lot of compute or take a long time to finish. So the question is how much of AI research is bottlenecked on thinking, versus experimental compute and other things you can’t speed up as easily.

My guess is that there’s quite a lot of room to accelerate the thinking and engineering parts. And then, as those get faster, you’d expect the bottleneck to shift toward running experiments. Better researchers can also make those experiments more efficient, though, so that’s not necessarily a fixed limit.

r001.rationale: The response does not say AI researchers can work around the clock or complete more sequential experiments per year.

r002.rationale: It mentions sharing useful techniques across copies, but not transferable computational context when handing subtasks to faster, weaker AIs.

r003.rationale: It does not state that running instances faster reduces how many can run in parallel.

r004.rationale: It mentions parallel copies and information sharing, but not forking instances from shared context to reduce coordination overhead.

r005.rationale: It identifies compute-intensive or slow experiments as bottlenecks that can prevent more researchers from producing proportional speedups.

r006.rationale: It says a thousand researchers need not make progress a thousand times faster because they may pursue correlated ideas and some experiments take time.
